title: Characterization of nested Walsh parity-check filters in a single-photon eight-mode register on a cloud photonic processor
authors: Emma Tully, Jonathan Washburn, Megan Simons
abstract: We characterize two nested Walsh parity-check filters implemented on Quandela's Belenos cloud photonic processor in a single-photon eight-mode spatial register. The modes are indexed by the vertices of the cube $Q_3$. The filters realize the classical $[8,7,2]$ single-parity-check code, the zero-sum neutral subspace $\mathcal{N}$ and the $[8,4,4]$ extended Hamming code, the parity-checked subspace $\mathcal{S}\subset\mathcal{N}$ with one DC and three face-parity syndrome channels. These are first-quantized path/mode encodings of classical codes: the experiment verifies leakage suppression and syndrome routing, not error correction or protection against photon loss, and all probabilities are conditional on postselected single-photon detections. Across more than 340,000 detections, neutral inputs show residual DC-port leakage of $0.02\%$-$1.1\%$ (mean $0.6\%$), corresponding to $\approx21\times$ suppression relative to the ideal $0.125$ DC-capture baseline and $31.6\times$ relative to the measured non-neutral control. Injected DC contamination gives a monotonic soft error signal, and the three face-parity syndrome channels route to their predicted ports with $94$-$99\%$ selectivity. A sector-preserving unitary core keeps leakage far below non-neutral controls over one to three applications, with differences dominated by calibration and compilation systematics rather than gate-cycle physics. We quantify these limits, including fixed-pattern separator bias, $\pm 0.02$ calibration offsets, and compilation scatter near the $10^{-3}$ leakage level, and report a Hong-Ou-Mandel degradation episode in which suppression vanished and recovered after recalibration.
summary: The research characterizes the implementation of nested Walsh parity-check filters on an eight-mode photonic processor to encode and protect single-photon states. By measuring leakage suppression and syndrome routing fidelity across hundreds of thousands of shots, the authors validate the feasibility of using such hardware for quantum error correction primitives. This work advances the understanding of physical limitations in scaling fault-tolerant quantum computation.
main_problem: The paper characterizes the faithful implementation of nested Walsh parity-check filters on a photonic processor to encode and protect quantum states in a single-photon eight-mode register.
main_result: They successfully demonstrated high fidelity for subspace projection, achieving significant suppression factors ($\approx 21	imes$) for residual leakage compared to ideal baselines, while confirming the structure of syndrome routing channels.
method: The methodology involves performing single-photon measurements on a cloud photonic processor, testing the physical realization of abstract quantum error-correcting codes (like the extended Hamming code) via path/mode encodings.
model_or_system: The system uses a single-photon eight-mode spatial register indexed by the vertices of a 3-cube ($Q_3$) on Quandela's Belenos processor. The encoding realizes subspaces corresponding to classical codes, such as the zero-sum neutral subspace and the $[8,4,4]$ extended Hamming code.
key_observables: Residual DC-port leakage (mean $0.6\%$), selectivity of face-parity syndrome channels ($94$-$99\%$), and Hong-Ou-Mandel visibility degradation/recovery.
important_parameters: Number of detections ($>340,000$); suppression factors ($\approx 21	imes$); fixed-pattern separator bias ($\pm 0.02$).
main_assumptions: The measurements are conditional on postselected single-photon detections and do not demonstrate full error correction or protection against photon loss.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the $Q_3$ vertex layout, the Gray-code Hamiltonian cycle ordering modes for the core, and show leakage/dump probabilities as a function of applied unitary depth or error injection strength.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first defining the theoretical encoding (nested filters realizing specific codes), then detailing the experimental setup on the photonic chip, followed by quantitative measurements of leakage suppression, syndrome routing fidelity, and diagnostic tests like HOM visibility degradation.
why_interesting: This work provides a crucial, highly detailed experimental benchmark for implementing abstract quantum error-correcting principles using near-term linear optical hardware, directly addressing resource limitations in physical realization.

figures.caption: FIG. 2. Experimental workflow for the single-photon hardware tests. A software-defined preparation unitary maps the injected single photon to a target neutral or parity-checked input state. Depending on the experiment, the prepared state is sent directly to a separator or first through d applications of the neutral-sector unitary core RN . BALANCE readout measures the DC leakage channel, while the parity separator routes the DC/sum and face-parity syndrome channels to output ports. All reported probabilities are normalized to postselected single-photon detections across the eight logical ports.

FIG. 3. Dump probability at the tested neutral-sector core depths on a logarithmic scale (Experiment 4). These are four operating-depth points (0, 1, 2, 3 applications) with a non-monotonic ordering, not a depth scan: no curve is fit through them and the figure should not be read as a depth-scaling trend (a dedicated ∼10–20 cycle scan, deferred to future work, would be required to extract a per-cycle leakage rate). Markers are the hardware values; vertical bars are 95% Wilson confidence intervals.
